newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - IPALCO bucks utility status quo.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - IPALCO bucks utility status quo.

text.p: IPALCO Enterprises Inc Chief Executive Officer John Hodowal, like the heads of other U.S. electric utilities, is maneuvering his company in a rapidly deregulated industry, but is bent on setting his own course.
Industry analysts view IPALCO, the holding company of Indianapolis Power and Light Co, as a maverick unafraid to take positions opposite those prevalent within the industry.
"Guilty," Hodowal admitted in a telephone interview with Reuters.
"We may be a maverick for proposing that the monopolistic activities (of other utilities) only give the illusion of customer choice."

IPALCO's most noticable breaks with convention are its call for federal rather than state legislation to set nationwide rules for deregulation, and its opposition to the recovery of stranded costs through bonds backed by customer surcharges.
Stranded costs refer to utilities' investments in assets like power plants back in the days when regulators allowed such costs to be passed down to the consumer.
"Electricity does not respect state borders. We could make transactions several states away," Hodowal said.
"This is not taking power from the states...This rankles some people because they have more influence over the states," he added.
Hodowal believes the positions held by most investor-owned utilities run counter to the spirit of competition.
"The reason (our position) is not popular is that the industry is run by companies charging customers twice the national average price for electricity," Hodowal said.

The national average is about seven cents per kilowatt hour. IPALCO says its electricity costs average about five cents per kilowatt hour for all of its 410,000 customers, most of whom are concentrated in and around Indianapolis, Ind.
IPALCO's 1996 revenues totaled $766 million.
Hodowal said high-cost utilities are still trying to force consumers to pay for past investments, especially in nuclear plants, which turned out to be costly mistakes.
"These people made decisions which turned out unfortunate or wrong," Hodowal said.
He rejected the argument that utilities should be allowed to recover stranded costs stemming from stricter environmental legislation or conservation measures.
"Virtually, all of us have to live under the same rules. Some of us live under the same rules with low rates and some with high rates," Hodowal said.

Analysts say IPALCO can afford to take contrary positions because it is a low-cost electricity producer set to snatch market share from high-cost utilities when all consumers eventually are allowed to shop around for the cheapest power.

"The main reason for this is that they have no stranded assets. They have low-cost generating plants. They think it's unfair that high-cost producers could still recover their (stranded) costs," said utility analyst Barry Abramson at Paine Webber in New York.
Over past two years, IPALCO has circulated position papers railing against securitization.
In its latest report, issued earlier this month, IPALCO called securitization a "swindle," pointing to faulty assumptions by utilities in calculating their stranded costs.
Furthermore, IPALCO's senior executives recently have testified against securitization before utility regulators in New York, Texas, Illinois, California, and Pennsylvania.

"They have taken an aggressive position to weaken others," said Michael Woods, a spokesman for PECO Energy Co, adding IPALCO's stance in Pennsylvania clearly is part of its plan to build up business in the state.
"We think in the future we will compete in Pennsylvania for customers," Hodowal said.

Philadelphia-based PECO Energy has requested permission from the Pennsylvania Public Utilities Commission to recover $4 billion from past investments in lines and power plants, arguing they will be uneconomic in a competitive marketplace.
Last month, the commission authorized PECO to recoup about $1 billion using so-called "transition bonds."
